area.name: Mount Landale
area.blurb: Mount Landale is a high summit on southern Vancouver Island above Cowichan Lake near Youbou, reached from a gated logging road and a lake basin. Its upper slopes are untrailed, with steep scrambling to the top.

route.name: Lomas Lake Route
route.rock_grade: Grade 3 scrambling with some very steep ground
route.best_season: Summer into early autumn, when the logging road is dry and the upper gully and ridge are clear of snow.
route.overview: The standard way up Mount Landale starts at a gate on a logging road above Cowichan Lake, follows a moderate trail to Lomas Lake, then leaves marked trail for a steep, largely unmarked climb to the col shared with El Capitan. A short ridge scramble finishes at the summit. Good route-finding and comfort on steep ground are needed.
route.beta: From the Cottonwood Main gate, follow the logging road about 6 km to the Lomas Lake trail and climb it by switchbacks to the lake. Beyond the lake there is no maintained path: head up a gully past an old mine working to a notch in the El Capitan-Landale col, then cross a small bench to gain the ridge and follow it to the top. A final short scramble leads to the summit cairn. The steepest scrambling is in the gully and on the upper ridge; look for the easiest line rather than forcing steep ground.
route.approach: Reach the Cottonwood Main gate on the Youbou-North Shore Road near Lake Cowichan. Walk the gated logging road about 6 km to the Lomas Lake trailhead; with a gate key and a high-clearance AWD or 4WD vehicle, about 8 km can be driven, saving a couple of hours of walking.
route.descent_text: Return the way you came: down the ridge, through the col notch and gully, then the Lomas Lake trail and logging road to the gate.
what_to_bring: Two or more litres of water
Navigation for the unmarked upper route
obj_haz: Weather change on the exposed ridge

road.driveNote: Leaves the Youbou-North Shore Road at a gate; about 6 km of road to the Lomas Lake trailhead.

area.name: Storelk Mountain
area.blurb: Storelk Mountain is a summit on the Continental Divide in the Elk Range, on the Alberta-British Columbia border near Highwood Pass. It is a difficult scramble with an untrailed approach in grizzly country.

route.name: East Face and Ridge
route.rock_grade: Class 4 on a steep, loose east face and an exposed ridge nose, with scree-covered slab
route.best_season: Summer through early autumn, once the face is free of snow; larch season in late September is popular.
route.overview: Storelk is a serious scramble rather than a walk. The approach has no trail and is a bushwhack through dense berry brush, then the route gains a col and climbs a loose east face and a steep ridge nose to the north-south summit ridge. The difficulty rating also reflects the approach, route-finding and bear country.
route.beta: Start in forest near Highwood Pass. A flagged ribbon at the start may lead to a false trail, so navigate carefully, cross the stream to its south side and climb steep slopes through dense berry bushes. A natural drainage leads up to the col. From the col, cross a meadow to the south and climb the steep, loose east face, detouring along the base of a short cliff band. Higher, a steep, exposed ridge nose reaches the main north-south ridge, which is followed over scree-covered slab, with several no-slip zones, to the summit. Parties using other lines, including the east ridge, have found the crest bushy and the ground steep and loose.
route.approach: Highwood Pass on Highway 40 in Kananaskis. The route starts in forest near the pass and quickly becomes a route-finding bushwhack; there is no maintained trail to the peak.
route.descent_text: Stay on the summit ridge rather than traversing below it across loose rubble and slab, then reverse the east face, taking care at the exposed step past the cliff band. A blazed trail marks the final stretch back to the road.
hazards: Class 4 exposed scrambling on loose rock
Rockfall from the loose east face
Grizzly bears in the approach brush
